questions.question: According to the passage, what is the primary aim of development testing?

options.A: To verify that the software meets performance benchmarks.
options.B: To discover bugs in the software.
options.D: To train end‑users on the system.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The text states that development testing is “primarily a defect testing process, where the aim of testing is to discover bugs in the software” [Page 41].

---

questions.question: Which statement best reflects a limitation of testing as expressed in the text?

options.A: Testing can prove that software has no defects.
options.B: Testing can guarantee correct behavior in every possible scenario.
options.C: Testing may miss some defects because a test could be overlooked.
options.D: Testing eliminates the need for future maintenance.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The passage explains that “testing cannot demonstrate that the software is free of defects… It is always possible that a test you have overlooked could discover further problems” [Page 36].

---

questions.question: Which of the following undesirable system behaviors is **not** listed by Dijkstra as something testing tries to root out?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Dijkstra’s quote lists “system crashes, unwanted interactions with other systems, incorrect computations, and data corruption” as undesirable behaviors; improved performance is not mentioned [Page 36].

---

questions.question: In the context of the passage, what is the purpose of “finding inputs or input sequences where the behavior of the software is incorrect, undesirable, or does not conform to its specification”?

options.A: To improve the user interface design.
options.B: To identify defects (bugs) in the software.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The text describes this activity as a way “to find inputs… where the behavior … is incorrect … These are caused by defects (bugs) in the software” [Page 36].

---

questions.question: Which activity is described as being “usually interleaved” with development testing?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The passage explicitly states that testing is “usually interleaved with debugging” [Page 41].

---

questions.question: The passage asserts that testing cannot demonstrate a certain condition about software. What is that condition?

options.A: That the software runs faster than a competitor’s product.
options.B: That the software is free of defects.
options.C: That the software has an intuitive user interface.
options.D: That the software meets all regulatory standards.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The text says “Testing cannot demonstrate that the software is free of defects” [Page 36].

---

questions.question: Which of the following examples of undesirable system behavior is explicitly mentioned in Dijkstra’s quoted statement?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Dijkstra lists “system crashes” among the undesirable behaviors [Page 36].

---

questions.question: When the passage describes testing as a “defect testing process,” which activity aligns most closely with that description?

options.B: Locating and fixing bugs in the code.
options.C: Discovering bugs through execution of test cases.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] A “defect testing process” focuses on discovering bugs, not on fixing them; fixing is part of debugging, which is interleaved but separate [Page 41].

---

questions.question: The statement that “it is always possible that a test you have overlooked could discover further problems” implies which of the following about any test suite?

options.A: It can be exhaustive and guarantee defect‑free software.
options.B: It may still miss defects despite thorough planning.
options.C: It eliminates the need for later maintenance activities.
options.D: It ensures compliance with all specifications.

questions.explanation: [Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The passage highlights the inherent incompleteness of testing, noting that overlooked tests can still reveal problems [Page 36].
